title: Three complete dialogues
description: Follow and take part in three real-life exchanges: meeting a neighbour, ordering at an eatery and taking an auto.

guide.title: How to use this unit
guide.text:
Each of the next three sections is a short conversation between two people, A and B, given line by line. Nothing in them is new grammar: every form has been taught in an earlier unit. Read each dialogue aloud several times, first as A and then as B, until you can say your lines without looking.

Things to notice as you read: the verb is always last; subjects are dropped when the verb ending makes them clear; yes/no questions end in a long -aa; and requests end in the polite -i.

The practice phrases below are the same lines, so the quiz will test whether you really understood each one.

examples.english: Hello.
Goodbye, I'm off.

guide.title: Dialogue 1: Meeting a neighbour
guide.text:
A is a long-time resident; B has just moved in. A opens with a guess ('are you new here?'), which is friendlier than a direct 'who are you?'. hosabaru is 'a new person' (from hosa, 'new'), in the respectful plural, and -aa makes it a question.

B answers with the past tense bande ('I came') and no pronoun. ooru is one's home town. In the last two lines A pays the standard compliment, and B gives the standard modest reply with the continuous form kaleetiddeeni, 'I am learning'.

Lines: A, B, A, B, A, B.

examples.english: A: Hello, are you new here?
B: Yes, I came last week.
A: Which is your home town?
B: I'm from London.
A: You speak Kannada well!
B: No, I'm learning now.

guide.title: Dialogue 2: At a small eatery
guide.text:
A is the person at the counter of a darshini, the stand-up eateries found all over Bengaluru; B is the customer.

enu kodali? is 'what shall I give?' - the -ali form used with a question word. B orders with numbers and kodi. kudiyoke is the -oke form of kudi: 'to drink, for drinking'. In A's last line, two questions with -aa give the either/or choice: 'will you eat right here, or will you take it away?'. B answers with tinteeni and then asks the bill with eshtaaytu?, 'how much did it come to?'.

Lines: A, B, A, B, A, B.

examples.english: A: What can I get you?
B: Two idlis and one vada, please.
A: What would you like to drink?
B: One coffee, less sugar.
A: Will you eat here or take it away?
B: I'll eat here. How much is it?

guide.title: Dialogue 3: Taking an auto
guide.text:
A is the passenger, B the auto-rickshaw driver. A names the place with the 'to' ending (-kke after a name ending in -a) and asks barteeraa?, 'will you come?'. B agrees with the same verb in the 'I' form: barteeni.

eshtu aagutte? is 'how much will it be?'. meetar mele ippattu is 'twenty on top of the meter' - a common demand; mele is 'on, above'.

The last two lines are A's instructions during the ride: svalpa bega softens 'go fast', and ille edagade is 'right here, on the left side'.

Lines: A, B, A, B, A, A.

examples.english: A: Auto! Will you go to Jayanagar?
B: Yes, get in.
A: How much will it be?
B: Meter plus twenty.
A: All right, please go a bit fast.
A: Stop right here on the left.

phrases.note: Dialogue 1, B. No pronoun needed: bande can only be 'I came' here.
Dialogue 2, A. What the person serving asks.

phrases.english: Two idlis and one vada, please.
What would you like to drink?
Will you eat here or take it away?
phrases.note: Dialogue 2, A. In practice people say 'paarsel' for takeaway.

phrases.english: I'll eat here. How much is it?
Auto! Will you go to Jayanagar?
phrases.note: Dialogue 3, A. Jayanagar is a neighbourhood of Bengaluru.
Dialogue 3, B. The verb repeated in the 'I' form means 'yes'.
Dialogue 3, B. Twenty rupees more than the meter shows.

phrases.english: All right, please go a bit fast.
Stop right here on the left.
